items.en: Since we launched Prime Agent [1] in August, it has been downloaded more than 300,000 times and has processed over 8 trillion tokens. Today, we're excited to ship a faster, cleaner and more reliable Prime Agent, rewritten from the ground up in Rust.

Over two weeks, Prime Agent orchestrated a swarm of over 2,000 agents to rewrite itself end to end, operating across 10,000+ Prime Sandboxes with over 200 billion tokens from Prime Inference’s GLM-5.3 endpoint. The Rust rewrite stress-tested Prime Agent’s multi-agent capabilities, including the sandbox and inference infrastructure we’ve been building to power large-scale agent swarms, autonomous research, and reinforcement learning.

To ensure feature parity with the TypeScript version, Prime Agent orchestrated subagents to topologically sort dependencies, with finite state machines structuring looped computations and correctness checks. In parallel, we rewrote the code architecture for easier maintenance and development. We then used runtime benchmarks and real Prime Agent traces to hillclimb performance metrics and triage bugs. Now, Prime Agent runs faster and uses fewer resources than most coding agent harnesses.

TypeScript helped us ship Prime Agent quickly, but its types are optional and disappear at runtime, errors travel as unchecked exceptions, CPU-heavy work like rendering and parsing large sessions competes with keyboard input on a single event loop, and every process pays for a JavaScript runtime and garbage collector. We want to keep shipping as fast as we do, while holding the code to a higher standard as it grows, and Rust suits that well:
- Performance: Prime Agent is a long-running daemon with a worker process per session, and native code without a garbage collector accounts for most of the memory and startup gains we’ve made.

- Concurrency: one daemon streams model output, runs tool calls, relays messages between agents and serves every attached client at once. Rust's Send andSync traits let the compiler check which data can move between threads and which can be shared.

- Compile-time guarantees: exhaustive enums, ownership and lifetimes rule out whole classes of bugs before the code runs, and Clippy's pedantic lints add hundreds more checks, which matters when agents write most of the code.

In addition to these clear performance gains, the rewrite gives us the opportunity to rethink our design choices. We have significantly modularized our codebase, and are reaping the rewards of this rewrite, including Windows support, session crash isolation, and a more consistent daemon protocol.

Our goal was for agents to perform the rewrite autonomously with as little human intervention as possible. Thus, the human work required was to setup proper verification to enable autonomous deployment at scale. We followed similar setup to previous work on automatic Rust translation [2]. Each specification covered a different kind of parity:

- TUI parity: a differential test suite compares the TypeScript and Rust binaries side by side against the same scripted model and diffs the terminal frames each one renders. It covers user flows, including launch, slash menus, tool calls, compaction, agents view, session resume, subagents and crash recovery.
- Harness parity: the same run diffd session transcripts and the requests each binary sends to the model provider, so both produce the same sessions from the same inputs.
- Protocol parity: all message types in the daemon protocol are checked against the TypeScript implementation, ensuring our ACP and daemon protocol APIs are consistent.
- Feature parity: since scripted flows cannot cover an entire interface, agents audited the TypeScript product component by component, classifying each as matching, partial or missing.

With an objective check for every kind of parity, the agents could measure their own progress and catch regressions before changes merged, which let us cut back on human review. Remaining bugs and behavior differences were largely found through internal use, which guided our follow-up work on missing features, reliability and interface polish.

We ran all orchestrators and their agents on two 8-core on-demand CPU nodes, each supporting over 100 concurrent subagents and their respective CPython kernels. Additionally, since compilation, type-checking and diffing would saturate any single machine when dozens of agents are running at once, we built out utilities for our agents to outsource heavy work to Prime Sandboxes, allowing us to heavily parallelize our port.

A single root agent orchestrated the rewrite and divided the work into a topological ordering of tasks. The root agent wrote no product code, keeping it free to monitor every task, merge finished work, and maintain an overview of the rewrite while working with us on priorities and decisions. We also kept generation and verification in separate agents, since an agent that writes code is biased when evaluating it. Therefore, each task assigned by the orchestrator moved through four agents:
- Planner: creates overall machine specification, including the feature design, ground-truth TypeScript behavior, and verifier (parity check)
- Implementer: writes the Rust code in a dedicated worktree so features can develop in parallel.
- Reviewer: inspects the pull request adversarially, using a different model and in a separate context from the implementer, looking for reasons the change is wrong.
- Verifier: compiles and runs the feature's parity checks and tests in a fresh Prime Sandbox.

A failed review or verification sends the feature back to the implementer with the findings, and the PR merges once both pass. We are building this pattern into Prime Agent to orchestrate a factory of finite state machines, so workflows like this one can be defined once, reused, and updated.
Porting to Rust also gave us a chance to restructure the codebase. This is where much of the long-term benefit comes from:

- Modularity: the code is split into nine crates with a one-way dependency graph that Cargo enforces, and the TUI’s only internal dependency is the shared types crate. The largest source file is now ~2,500 lines, down from ~15,000 in TypeScript, with no files over 5,000 lines compared with four in TypeScript.

- Isolation: each session runs in its own worker process under a small supervisor, so a failure in one session leaves the others running, and sessions persist on disk so clients can reattach after a restart.

- Platform abstraction: transport, process control and file locking sit behind platform-specific interfaces, so something like Windows support came down to implementing those traits rather than rewiring the daemon.
- One protocol definition: the client, the daemon and every worker compile against the same message types in the shared types crate, so a change to the protocol is checked everywhere it is used.
- Catalog-driven models: ported our model and MCP lists to a separate catalog fetched at runtime, allowing us to ship new models and plugins without a Prime Agent release.

While the autonomous workflow went further than we expected, the parity checks only verified the behavior they exercised. Once parity on the main RLM loop was achieved, we moved all our rewrite agents onto Rust, allowing us to dogfood the Rust version at scale (and now Prime Agent Rust was recursively improving itself!). Later, we moved our internal team onto the Rust build for daily use, which exposed bugs and missing behavior outside the coverage of the differential tests. Throughout our dogfood cycles, we had agents review logs and traces from all beta users, allowing us to automatically diagnose and resolve runtime and agent issues identified by users. We also took the rewrite as an opportunity to redesign some of the UX/TUI flows and model-facing API.

Bringing the rewrite to release quality took follow-up work over the following weeks, from finishing feature ports and fixing bugs to improving performance and polishing the interface. Prime Agent still wrote and tested these changes, while we had humans in the loop involved in finding problems, directing the changes, and reviewing all results.

With feature parity achieved, we wanted to optimize Prime Agent runtime performance across all user flows. We approached it the same way as the rewrite: by giving the agents an objective way to measure their own progress. We built a benchmark harness that measures Prime Agent performance across a variety of runtime metrics, and let Prime Agent hillclimb its speed and resource usage with well-deliberated improvements.

The performance benchmark evaluates Prime Agent in Rust and TypeScript, as well as other agent harnesses, on a fresh 4-core, 8 GB Prime Sandbox per benchmark, with noise checks that withhold any result too unstable to compare. Agents run in a real terminal driven through a screen emulator against a scripted model, so timings reflect what a user sees and exclude inference.

With the harness in place, a second orchestrator ran a hillclimbing loop for three days with a single objective: improve the benchmark results without breaking parity. Each experiment followed the same procedure:
- Agents profile the benchmarks to find where time and memory go, turning the largest costs into a backlog of hypotheses that the orchestrator then assigns to workers.
- Workers build the current code and the candidate change on the same sandbox and run them in alternating order, along with neighboring benchmarks to catch regressions elsewhere.

- Two reviewer agents, each on a different frontier model, check that behavior still matches TypeScript, that output stays byte-identical wherever the change claims it, and that nothing regresses on the model-facing surface.
- The change merges, and the next experiment measures from the new baseline.

We deliberately gave the loop no numeric targets, since a fixed threshold tends to become a stopping point. The agents' only objective was to keep improving the benchmarks without breaking parity for as long as measurable gains remained. Over the hillclimb cycle, the loop logged over 144 experiment and audit records, merging over 69 valid changes that boosted performance. Below are some significant improvements we’ve seen in important areas:

Most of the gains came from three kinds of change: moving work off the startup and render paths, replacing polling loops with event-driven waits, and releasing memory as soon as large sessions finished loading.

Overall, our Rust rewrite and following performance hillclimbing has made Prime Agent significantly faster and more resource efficient. With time to input roughly 14x faster than TypeScript and using over 80% less memory after startup, Prime Agent is amongst the fastest coding agent harnesses available.
External harness results were measured with our custom runtime suite. Without a common benchmark standard, comparisons should be interpreted with caution.
This more modular codebase and stronger compile-time checks will also help us ship new capabilities faster and catch more mistakes before they reach users.

With our Rust port in, we’re bringing the same attention to detail to every part of Prime Agent, from everyday systems interactions to complex work cross many agents. Now that infrastructural improvements are out of the way, we are accelerating on capabilities and evals, and making the multi-agent workflows behind this rewrite available to you.

Prime Agent will also be more tightly knit into the Prime Intellect ecosystem, allowing you to work across the stack with cloud agent swarms, inference, traces, sandboxes, evals, hosted training, and more.
With this rewrite, we are also releasing Prime Agent with native Windows support (beta) and installation through homebrew. Prime Agent remains open source and installs with one command:
curl -fsSL https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.sh | sh
irm https://app.primeintellect.ai/prime-agent/install.ps1 | iex
If you'd like to work on Prime Agent, we are hiring.

Anthropic said its models exploited websites on the internet, including some run by U.S. government agencies, and it will turn off live internet access for all of its internal evaluations until the frontier lab is sure it can monitor and control its AI agents.

The incidents, disclosed in a blog post, involved AI agents tasked to solve problems seeking resources on the internet. In the process, they exploited software flaws, avoided paywalls and anti-bot restrictions, used URL shortening services to smuggle information pass restrictions, and even submitted a false murder tip to the Philadelphia police.
Anthropic said it discovered these new issues in a review of its model’s activities that began in July, underscoring the lab’s lack of awareness of its software’s behavior.

Notably, the company said that alignment training was not yet sufficient for skills like search and computer use that are central to its pitch that AI agents will be used by any professional who relies on digital tools.

The behaviors Anthropic disclosed are similar to incidents involving OpenAI agents that collaborated to break into various websites in search of information, including some run by the Australian government.

Anthropic previously disclosed that its models had broken into external systems. The frontier lab said it considered today’s disclosures “significantly less severe from an alignment and security perspective” than those it announced before.
However, the lab still said it had “turned off live internet access” for “all our internal evaluations” until it is certain it can monitor and control its agents.

It’s not clear what that means, but Sydney Von Arx, the founder of Nightingale, an AI safety organization, told TechCrunch in an interview before this disclosure that developing models on a data center cut off from the open internet would be very challenging for researchers to use, and for the progress of the models, which benefit from internet access.
“You have to align them at some point,” Von Arx said. “If the AIs are released to production and never have access to the internet, that’s not a very useful tool.”

Anthropic said the behavior was a result of flaws in the lab’s training environments, which led the models to believe they would be rewarded for finding loopholes or avoiding restrictions, a behavior called “reward hacking.”

The company said it would stop running some of its evaluations or move them offline, and has built tooling to detect and block this behavior. This tooling was tested against the kind of incidents disclosed today and blocked them; it’s not clear what evidence will prompt Anthropic to return live internet access to its internal evaluations.

Anthropic also said it would migrate its internal AI agents to “centrally managed infrastructure with strong containment,” and is beginning to using safety classifiers more frequently to monitor those agents.
We’re putting too much faith in AI’s ability to say no

Today’s AI models are trained to refuse a vast number of prompts. If you ask your chatbot how to poison a colleague or how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down. But refusal fails, sometimes horrifically.

Some people are attempting to use AI to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms. Sooner or later, failed refusals may result in global calamity. What’s more, relying on refusal means drawing a line between what a model should obey and what it must disobey.

Governments will also get to draw their own lines, potentially restricting free speech. At the same time, the capabilities that make AI useful could also make it dangerous. If we want it to help cure cancer, AI needs genetics expertise that could also produce bioweapons.
We’re still figuring out the side effects of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs

This week my colleague Antonio Regalado reported on new research suggesting GLP-1 drugs may slow biological aging. It’s the latest in a raft of potential benefits associated with these drugs. But there are also some weird side effects.
The most common are gastrointestinal, but researchers are also investigating possible links to hair loss, nail disorders and damage to the nerves behind the eye.
10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Envision Energy and its global ambitions for wind power

China is installing wind turbines faster than any other country. One of its leading manufacturers, Envision Energy, is integrating renewable energy into data centers, using wind turbines to generate power and batteries to store it on-site.

Recently, it became the first company to directly power a data center entirely with renewable energy. An AI-powered system optimizes the power output so the facility can receive a steady supply, regardless of whether the wind is blowing. Now, it wants to bring that approach to data centers in deserts around the world.

A year after my rapist was found responsible following a Title IX investigation by Cornell University, rumors about the rape of my fellow student now known as Jane Doe began to spread on campus. We all knew that something bad had happened; we’d received a crime-alert email of a “sexual assault” involving a woman and “several males.” There were whispers about a fraternity group chat, a horrific message advertising “free pussy.” But that was all we heard, and news of the case faded with time. Needless to say, I was just as shocked as the rest of the world to learn the outcome.

Hearing Jane Doe’s story, I couldn’t help but feel as if I’d been fooled by the institution that was supposed to protect me. After a grueling Title IX investigation, my assailant was found responsible for my sexual assault in March 2023. His punishment? He received a “written reprimand,” was ordered to write a “reflection paper,” and was placed on behavioral probation until he graduated two months later.

For the past three years, I believed that his punishment was so light because my rape wasn’t significant or bad enough. I wasn’t drugged; he used no weapons. In the verdict issued in my case, the investigators wrote it didn’t seem like my rapist “acted maliciously.” I thought, Surely if my rape had “been worse,” the punishment would have fit the crime.

However, I realize now that I was not the only Cornell student failed by Title IX. It was not a singular case of misjudgment or a bug in the system. Rather, the university has put our assailants’ futures and their potential above our lives. This apparent pattern of “essays for rape” unravels the narratives we are told about sexual violence and accountability, illuminating the real cause behind the lack of justice for survivors.

I didn’t want to report my rape. I didn’t want my entire life to be dissected by investigators, to have the worst thing that has ever happened to me turned into evidence, and to be forced to provide my pain as “proof.” I didn’t want to spend Valentine’s Day of my sophomore year testifying in front of my rapist or being cross-examined by his counselor. Yet I did.

I was compelled to do so because I knew if he never faced any punishment, he would never have to reckon with that night and his actions. He was 28 years old and about to receive his graduate degree. He would have been allowed to rewrite it as a bad hookup, a forgettably unenjoyable night. If he thought of me at all, he may have remembered me as a crazed girl who forgot she gave consent or a 19-year-old who was embarrassed.
I didn’t have the choice to forget, to reframe that night for myself. To me, he is forever my rapist. I cannot know the rest of my life as anything except the aftermath of rape.

I know that I am one of many. In a country where the president has been held liable for sexual abuse, we are all too familiar with the brutal reality of how often perpetrators evade accountability. Yet as the news of Jane Doe’s lawsuit against her seven alleged rapists and Cornell University reverberated across the world, many were horrified by not only the unfathomably disgusting nature of the crime alleged but the egregiously empty response by the university. Five of the seven assailants were assigned to write an essay as punishment for allegedly drugging and raping Jane Doe in their fraternity house in the fall of 2024.

The response by Cornell University to both Jane Doe’s case and mine begs us to consider that the lack of justice for sexual-assault survivors is not necessarily an issue of believability but an issue of care. Do we care enough about survivors?

This lack of care is evidenced by the essay assignments, but it’s also in the structure of Title IX itself. There are nearly 26,000 students at Cornell but just three full-time investigators in the Title IX office. Cornell reports that 11 percent of students, approximately 2,860 people, are sexually assaulted each year. Even if only 10 percent of those victims reported, a single investigator would have a caseload of 95 per year. For the same body of students, there is one full-time victim advocate. With minimal time and resources to appropriately address the student demand, they are spread too thin, and a mere 25 percent of students are aware that the program exists at all. (In response to an inquiry about the similarities between my case and Jane Doe’s, a spokesperson for the university declined to comment citing federal privacy laws).
What Jane Doe, what I, and what every survivor deserves is care — a care that leads to a system of accountability and is capable of providing justice.

After my rape, I became constantly terrified that no one could hear me, that no one was truly listening. I resented the sound of my voice and what my body looked like in the mirror. I became afraid that the only thing I will ever be, all that I am, is a body.

Any beauty in my life now is not a measure of “how bad” getting raped was but a testament to my own persistence to continue living. In the time since my rape, I have felt everything there is to feel. I let myself be bad; I let myself be good. I find joy in spite of him. I am strong in spite of him. I grow in spite of him, I learn in spite of him, I love in spite of him, I am loved in spite of him, I exist in spite of him.

As Jane Doe’s lawsuit is litigated, I hope people will see, hear, watch, and speak about the case. But more than anything, I hope people will allow the anger, disgust, sadness, and grief to move them in such a way that they begin to truly care about these injustices.

When is a movie more than a movie? When it’s Digger, the Tom Cruise vehicle that bombed spectacularly in theaters last week like the last burst of light from a dying star. Digger, which cost a reported $150 million, is the final feature to be released by Warner Bros. before the century-old studio gets folded into a larger media behemoth that will known as Skydance, and as such, its failure has become thematically load-bearing. Though it wasn’t the reason co-chairs Pam Abdy and Mike DeLuca were pushed out, it capped off a run of rough releases under their leadership this year, a reminder that the same willingness to bet on big swings that yielded Sinners and Weapons also yielded Maggie Gyllenhaal’s unfortunate The Bride! If you’d like, you can see Digger’s defeat as proof of movie stars’ fading appeal or the difficulty in selling audiences on original material or an increasing corporate intolerance for criticism of the wealthy and powerful. But if we’re going to stuff Digger with all that baggage, it only seems fair we do the same to another movie bookending the merger — Matchbox: The Movie, which lands on Apple TV today.

We’ll never know if Matchbox: The Movie is a flop because it went straight to streaming, a black box of viewership info. I doubt most people will even register that the movie exists. But while it may not have cost $150 million, it obviously wasn’t cheap because it’s an action comedy full of car chases and vehicles flipping through the air and it stars John Cena as CIA agent Sean Walker, who involuntarily involves his childhood friend group in a globe-trotting adventure. And it is bad. Not in the way some people think Digger (which I’m actually kind of fond of) is bad, where someone — like director Alejandro González Iñárritu — had a vision that really didn’t work. Matchbox: The Movie is bad in that aimless way where it is clear that no one, from director Sam Hargrave (Extraction) to writer David Coggeshall to the dozens of actors and hundreds of crew members, knows why they’re there, other than to collect a paycheck. No one involved in Matchbox: The Movie seems like they’d be able to make a case for why the movie exists, which makes you wonder why on earth anyone would watch it.

Matchbox: The Movie stinks in a thousand relatively minor and noncommittal ways that end up feeling so much worse than a grand and more personal disaster would. It never figures out what it means to make a movie based on a line of toy cars nor conveys why those toy cars are meaningful. It barely gives us a chance to see how the group of middle-schoolers the story starts with bond over and play with the cars — maybe because they’ve already outgrown the practice by then with young Sean having moved on to a fierce crush on fellow member Aimee. Then Sean moves away and grows up to become a spy who, after wrapping up a mission involving smuggling a nuclear warhead for reasons unknown, decides to pay an impromptu visit to his tweenage buddies. At that point, they’re all drugged and black-bagged by the incoming CIA director of operations (played by Corey Stoll, no less), who believes Sean stole the warhead and immediately resorts to beatings to get its whereabouts out of him.

Aimee (Jessica Biel), Crosby (Sam Richardson), Ted (Arturo Castro), and Charmaine (Teyonah Parris) go from acting inexplicably suspicious of Sean and his motives despite the kidnapping and torture to just as abruptly deciding they need to stick by his side and risk everything to help him out. The movie is initially squirrelly about violence in a way that suggests it was first conceived as a family-friendly enterprise with Sean pointedly not killing the people he fights and taking flak from Aimee for wanting to shoot people. However, by the end, he’s blowing up dudes with grenades while delivering quips like the star of an ’80s muscle movie. Though it’s tempting to read these tonal switchbacks as signs of studio mangling, it doesn’t feel like there was much vision to be messed with in the first place. Matchbox: The Movie is filled with bits that never quite add up to the jokes they’re meant to be, like Crosby’s love for the Leatherman he always carries, but its attempts at emotional appeal are also strange and generic; it’s hard to invest in characters still extremely stuck on who they were in middle school. Maybe you just can’t hope for much from a movie inspired by a line of toy cars. At least Masters of the Universe, the previous Mattel adaptation, had lore to pull from.

That raises the question of why Matchbox: The Movie was considered a worthwhile bet at all. It was produced by Skydance Corporation CEO David Ellison, a man who — thanks to the efforts of his father, Larry, one of the richest people in the world, and the series of corporate consolidations they engineered — is now one of the most powerful media moguls around. And Matchbox: The Movie is an example of Ellison’s general approach to films, one that will shape the 30 he’s promised to put in theaters each year. It’s an approach centered on IP, on remakes and adaptations and legacy sequels. That’s no longer what, a few years ago, might have been described as a cautious approach, not when audiences are making out-of-nowhere titles like Obsession and Backrooms into buzzy hits and craving something new. But it’s safe in another way. While Digger tried for something, Matchbox: The Movie aims for nothing — it can’t really fail because there are no expectations. It can only pleasantly surprise by being tolerable, but in this case, it’s really not. If this utterly uninspired movie deserves to get attention, it’s only as a potential key text to what the new Frankensteined Skydance Corporation is likely to give us in the future, especially with Ellison having brought on former Mattel CEO Ynon Kreiz to co-run the company: projects that are built on brand synergy and an assumption of nostalgia and don’t try at all.

Darializa Avila Chevalier was at a community meeting in Harlem on Thursday afternoon when her phone began blowing up with news that plainclothes federal immigration officers had just shot a man in his car in Marble Hill, the northernmost Manhattan neighborhood. Avila Chevalier, the likely next congresswoman for the district, rushed to the scene on West 225th Street and began asking the NYPD about which federal agency had shot 28-year-old Oscar Belgal in the neck as a 5-year-old was in the back seat. “We were told a number of agencies, but the only ones that I was able to see any kind of identification for was HSI,” she says, referring to Homeland Security Investigations. “There were a number of plainclothes agents, who we believe were ICE agents, walking around.”

Minutes after the shooting, protesters rushed in to demand that federal officers — including an agent in a construction vest with a long gun — leave the scene and the city. Avila Chevalier went with demonstrators across the Spuyten Duyvil Creek into Inwood, where Belgal had been taken to Allen Hospital. On the protest line, she says, “police just began escalating. It was truly just chaos.” The congressional candidate says she was trying to get between protesters and the police when an officer threw her to the ground. “My arm and my lower back hurt for most of the evening,” she says. “Thankfully, I’m okay today, but it was a pretty aggressive push.” Four protesters were arrested.

Months after President Donald Trump’s deportation czar, Tom Homan, promised to flood the city with ICE agents, New York is now facing its biggest immigration test yet in the second Trump administration. On Thursday night, Mayor Zohran Mamdani described the shooting as an “outrage” and repeated his call to abolish ICE. The next morning, he spent two hours on the phone with President Trump and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin; he urged them to release Belgal, a Dominican national who had previously been arrested for grand larceny. But the call didn’t have the desired result. Before Belgal’s hearing on Friday afternoon, even his lawyers said they did not know where he was within ICE’s deportation machine. At a press conference, Mullin criticized Mamdani, claiming his calls to abolish ICE “incite hostility.” He also came to the defense of federal agents, saying they didn’t know a child was in the car when they put seven bullets in it.

Mamdani, once again, is being squeezed between critics on the right and his base of support on the left. In a statement on Friday, Avila Chevalier called for the resignation of NYPD commissioner Jessica Tisch. “The NYPD spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers,” the candidate wrote. She was also concerned that the commissioner, in a press conference on Thursday night, had referred to Bengal’s grand-larceny guilty plea in 2023. “What was incredibly appalling to me was that after all of this had transpired, the police commissioner, instead of condemning ICE’s actions, began vilifying the victim of its violence,” says Avila Chevalier. “To me, that was just so obscene and unacceptable. It was truly enraging, and it goes against the spirit, if not the letter, of our sanctuary policies that she is supposed to be upholding.

As for Mullin, Avila Chevalier — who will be one of the most left-leaning representatives in Congress next year — said his comments, including the claim that officers did not know a child was in the car, had the “stupidest line of logic.”

“If this was a targeted arrest, then they would have known who they were arresting,” she says. “They would have known that he was a father; they would have known where he was going and who might be with him. Plant-based diets are associated with many long-term health benefits, but for older adults, there may be a potential downside.
Eating a strictly vegetarian diet may make it harder to protect muscle mass as we age.
Protein is a key component in building, maintaining, and strengthening muscle, and in older age, you could need more of it than current guidelines suggest.
Vegetarians tend to eat less dietary protein than meat eaters, and recent research suggests that underweight vegetarians are less likely to live to 100.
Now, a new clinical trial adds a positive spin.
Among adults aged 55 and over, both vegetarians and meat eaters gained muscle and showed similar improvements in strength and physical performance after 12 weeks of resistance training.
The findings are published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.

"Importantly, our results also show that a predominantly plant-based diet can still support meaningful improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical function when protein intake is sufficiently high and combined with resistance training," write researchers at the Amsterdam University of Applied Sciences in the Netherlands.
In the randomized trial, 108 adults undertook either a vegetarian diet or an omnivorous diet for three months.
During the trial, they also partook in resistance training three times a week, with exercises including leg presses, squats, chest presses, lat pulldowns, arm pulls, and abdominal exercises.
Each participant was counseled on healthy eating plans and how to consume at least 1.2 grams of protein per kilogram of their body weight each day.
On average, both groups were successful in meeting their daily protein goals – even the vegetarians, who could not eat meat or fish, only dairy, eggs, or plant-based proteins.
By the end of the trial, muscle strength and physical performance improved in both groups, with no significant difference between vegetarians and meat eaters.
On leg presses, participants could lift more weight, and on chair stands, they stood up faster than they did when the trial first started.
But there was one key difference between the groups.

Muscle mass in the legs and arms increased in both vegetarians and omnivores during the trial, but omnivores showed about 70 percent more gains (+0.66 kilograms, compared to +0.38 kg for vegetarians).
It is not clear whether this is due to lower protein intake by vegetarians, or something about the quality of dietary protein provided by meat and other animal-based foods.
Interestingly, the study found that vegetarians who ate more protein tended to gain more muscle, whereas meat eaters who ate more protein didn't.
"The omnivorous group likely reached a saturating protein threshold where additional intake yielded no further anabolic benefit," the authors hypothesize.
Nutrition is a highly complex area of research subject to lifestyle, behavioral, genetic, social, and environmental factors too numerous to count.
This particular cohort of older adults was predominantly White, healthy, and highly educated. It is unclear if these findings are relevant to others.

Still, the results join other recent studies suggesting that vegetarian diets, as long as they provide enough calories and essential nutrients, can be associated with lives as long and as healthy as those of meat eaters.
Research like this is a good reminder that eating enough protein in older age is important, especially for vegetarians.
"The suitability of a more plant-based diet may depend on individual context," the authors of the new study conclude.

"For people with low appetite or low energy intake, extra focus on meeting protein targets and ensuring protein quality is likely needed to maintain muscle mass, which is particularly important for older adults."
The research has been published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.
BAE Systems has received a contract from Lockheed Martin to install an upgraded Block 4 electronic warfare system into new F-35 Joint Strike Fighters, as well as to retrofit some older jets.

BAE’s AN/ASQ-239 EW systems will be installed on lots 20 to 22 of the F-35, the company said in an Oct. 6 statement, and some older F-35s with previous versions of the EW system will be retrofitted to have the latest version installed.

“BAE Systems has been the EW supplier for the F-35 program for the past 21 years, successfully designing and developing the Block 1, Block 2, and Block 3 configurations” of the AN/ASQ-239, Amber Dolan, BAE’s vice president of F-35 solutions, said in a follow-up statement to Air & Space Forces Magazine. “We are currently developing Block 4 systems that can accelerate the delivery of advanced EW capabilities via adaptable hardware and incremental software updates.”

The updated EW suite is part of a broader program of upgrades to the Lockheed Martin-made F-35, collectively referred to as Block 4. Lockheed previously awarded BAE a $491 million contract for the F-35 EW systems in 2023, and another $493 million contract in 2021.
The Block 4 EW systems that will be in F-35 lots 20 and beyond “offer improvements in threat detection, situational awareness, and capabilities to counter modern threats,” Dolan said.

BAE declined to say how much the contract is worth and how many EW systems it will deliver for new jets and retrofits. The company said it has delivered more than 1,500 EW systems for the F-35 so far.

BAE said the AN/ASQ-239 system provides both offensive and defensive EW capabilities, which give pilots a 360-degree view of the battlefield and allow the F-35 to operate in environments protected by enemy fighters, missiles, drones, or integrated air defense systems. Its passive long-range sensing capabilities combine with high-speed signal processing and advanced algorithms to allow pilots to detect and counter threats before an enemy can act, the company said. The system’s software can also be quickly updated to account for new threats.

A previous upgrade to the AN/ASQ-239 EW system—called the Digital Channelized Receiver/Techniques Generator and Tuner Insertion Program, or DTIP—was launched in 2018. Those DTIP improvements allowed for previous versions of the EW system to be condensed into a smaller footprint that required less power, which created space for the new Block 4 modernization.

BAE said it has made investments in facilities—including the 2022 opening of a new 200,000-square-foot engineering and production facility in Manchester, N.H.—to help design and develop new EW systems. BAE also designs and manufactures EW systems at facilities in Merrimack, N.H., Nashua, N.H., and Austin, Texas.
This image from Copernicus Sentinel-2, acquired on 5 April 2026, shows the Etosha National Park in northern Namibia.
Zoom in to explore this image at its full resolution.
The area is a game reserve featuring a large salt flat – the Etosha Pan – as well as numerous smaller salt pans, with vegetation shown in red in this false-colour image.

The Etosha Pan, which spans roughly 130 km from east to west and covers 4760 sq km, appears bright white to human eyes. The colours in this image, however, range from the white expanses of salt to light blue where water contains cloudy sediment, and dark blue where the water is clearer.

The image was acquired at the beginning of the dry season, when average daily temperatures typically range from 14°C to 30°C. Water is also still present in the smaller salt pans that dot the landscape northwest of the Etosha Pan, the biggest of which is the Natukanaoka Pan. The water in these small ‘lakes’ appears in shades of green and blue.

The Ekuma river, near the centre of the image, is seen flowing from Lake Oponono at an elevation of about 1200 m above sea level, southwards to the salt flat at 1030 m. Lake Oponono is able to hold water from one wet season to the next and is a habitat for flamingos and cattle.

The vegetation surrounding the Etosha Pan – shown in striking red by Sentinel-2’s near-infrared channel – consists mainly of grassland, savannas and mopane woodland. Mopane trees are the dominant type of vegetation across the eastern and central areas of the national park, showing up as dark, vibrant red in this image. They provide a habitat for elephants, giraffe and leopards. The savannahs, in the west and southern areas of the park, are home to wildebeest, lions and springbok.

Patches of red are also visible on the Etosha Pan, suggesting vegetation is present. While few plants thrive in the salty clay terrain, some types of blue-green algae and salt-tolerant grasses have adapted to the harsh environment.

Sentinel-2 carries a multispectral imager, which detects light in 13 spectral bands – in contrast to the human eye, which can see only three spectral bands (red, blue and green). This allows the mission to capture near-infrared and short-wave infrared light, creating false-colour images that highlight specific features on the landscape. Since healthy plants reflect more near-infrared light, the areas with vibrant red correlate to areas where vegetation is dense.

SpaceX early Saturday will try again to launch a Falcon 9 rocket carrying a batch of data satellites for the U.S. military’s Space Development Agency (SDA), five days after a last-minute abort scrubbed the first attempt.

Liftoff from Vandenberg Space Force Base in California is scheduled for 12:39 a.m. PDT (3:39 EDT / 0739 UTC). The Falcon 9 will take a southerly trajectory on departure from Space Launch Complex 4E, currently SpaceX’s only launch facility on the West Coast.
Spaceflight Now will have live coverage starting about 30 minutes prior to launch.

Monday’s launch attempt was halted by an auto-abort with 58 seconds remaining on the clock. The halt was triggered moments after the rocket’s onboard computers took control of the countdown. SpaceX did not disclose the cause of the abort but in a social media post said: “Vehicle and payload are in good health, and teams are resetting for a launch attempt no earlier than tomorrow, October 6.”

However, the vehicle was lowered to a horizontal position at the pad, usually a sign of troubleshooting a hardware issue, and the launch was repeatedly pushed back a day at a time. A missile test from Vandenberg using the Western Test Range on Friday might have contributed to the launch finally settling on Saturday.

The mission, dubbed Tranche 1 Transport Layer A (T1TL-A), is the fourth mission sending production satellites into orbit for the SDA. This is one piece of a broad constellation — called the Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture (PWSA) — designed to support the U.S. military and its allies through space-based capabilities, like missile tracking and secure communications.
The mission will use Falcon 9 first stage booster B1103. This will be its sixth flight following the launches of the SDA’s T1TL-E, NROL-179, and three batches of Starlink satellites.
Less than 7.5 minutes after liftoff, SpaceX plans to land B1103 at Landing Zone 4. If successful, this will be the 37th landing at LZ-4 and the 668th Falcon booster landing to date.

The T1TL-A mission is one of 23 missions awarded to SpaceX as part of the National Security Space Launch (NSSL) Phase 2 contract awarded in August 2020, which is managed by the U.S. Space Force’s Space Systems Command (SSC). The previous missions from the SDA have already been launched:

The T1TL-B and -E missions featured satellites manufactured by York Space Systems and the T1TL-C satellites were produced by Lockheed Martin. Space Force Col. Ryan Hiserote, SSC’s division chief in Assured Access to Space, told Spaceflight Now back in September 2025 that these initial T1TL missions could be launched in any order.
The 21 satellites flying as part of the T1TL-A mission were manufactured by Northrop Grumman and delivered to Vandenberg Space Force Base on Sept. 28.

Tranche 1 is the initial component of the PWSA constellation is expected to begin providing operational capabilities to the Department of Defense beginning in 2027. When complete, T1 will consist of 126 Transport Layer satellites, 28 Tracking Layer satellites, and four missile defense demonstration spacecraft.
With the three launches completed to date, there are 63 satellites in orbit.

“In close coordination with Space Systems Command (SSC) and Space Launch Delta 30, the deployment of Tranche 1’s proliferated capability will soon deliver continuous overwatch—neutralizing any first-mover advantage by delivering data to warfighters around the world, nearly instantaneously,” said GP Sandhoo, SDA Director and Space Force Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Missile Warning and Tracking following the T1TL-E launch in July.

The SDA said the Transport Layer will consist of between 300 to 500 satellites in low Earth orbit from 750 km to 1,200 km in altitude. The SDA said once complete, 95 percent of the globe will be in view of at least two of the T1TL satellites at any given time.

“The constellation will be interconnected with Optical Inter-Satellite Links (OISLs) which have significantly increased performance over existing radio frequency crosslinks,” the SDA wrote. “LEO orbits in conjunction with OISLs will reduce path loss issues but more importantly offer much lower latencies, which are deemed critical to prosecute time sensitive targets in today’s wartime environment.”
These satellites will be able to integrate with the Link-16 and Integrated Broadcast System (IBS) to allow for “timely threat warnings and situational awareness information”.
The launches of these satellites are managed by the SSC’s System Delta 80 (SYD 80) and the Space Fore Portfolio Acquisition Executive for Assured Access to Space.

A newly released panorama captured by NASA’s Curiosity rover offers the most detailed view yet of distant, wind-carved Martian cliffs, highlighting features the mission’s scientists have long been waiting to see up close. The scene was snapped at 8:30 a.m. local Mars time, showing striking blue hues in the foreground as bright morning light illuminates crags known as yardangs on the horizon.

The panorama was captured by Curiosity’s Mastcam on Aug. 11, the 4,982nd Martian day, or sol, of the mission, and comprises six individual images that were stitched together after being sent to Earth. Unlike most of Curiosity’s Mastcam images, this one was processed without white balancing, preserving the early morning appearance.

The yardang layer extends roughly 10 miles (16 kilometers) across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp, a 3-mile-tall (5-kilometer-tall) mountain that Curiosity has been ascending since 2014. In fact, the rover recently passed another milestone in its ascent, reaching 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) of elevation — the most ever climbed on Mars. As it draws ever-closer to the yardangs, mission scientists expect to get even more amazing imagery — and, they hope, answers to how these cliffs were created.

Mount Sharp is made up of layers, each recording a distinct period of Mars’ history. By studying them, scientists have been able to learn more about lakes and streams that covered this part of the Red Planet billions of years ago. Eventually, the water dried up and left salty minerals behind. After new material stopped settling on the mountain, some of it may have been stripped away by wind, giving rise to the yardangs.

“The yardang layer looks out of place. It’s the wrong color, the layers tilt at an odd angle, and it almost appears plastered on,” said Ashwin Vasavada, Curiosity project scientist of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California. “But that’s what makes it exciting to reach. No one is sure exactly what created this layer, but one idea is it may be ash deposited by ancient volcanic eruptions.”

Curiosity is in the second year of its fifth extended mission, which started with an exploration of the spiderweb-like boxwork ridges. The rover will spend most of the next year or so driving through layers enriched with sulfates and carbonates, both signs of ancient drying on the surface. Sometime in 2027, scientists hope to reach the base of the yardangs, where Curiosity will be able to use its robotic arm to collect one-of-a-kind data on these mysterious features.
From Mars to the Milky Way — never miss a discovery! Delivered straight to your inbox.

Curiosity was built by NASA JPL, which is managed by Caltech in Pasadena, California. NASA JPL leads the mission on behalf of the agency’s Science Mission Directorate in Washington as part of its Mars Exploration Program portfolio. Malin Space Science Systems in San Diego built and operates Mastcam.

In 1957, the economist and journalist Barbara Ward gave the first of the Aggrey-Fraser-Guggisberg Memorial Lectures at the University College of Ghana. Shortly after Kwame Nkrumah led the British colony of the Gold Coast towards self-government, he invited Ward to address the independent country’s first cohort of students. Ward was well acquainted with the local political landscape because she had spent the previous four years living in the Gold Coast, witnessing its political transformation. As the world’s eyes were set on Ghana, the first sub-Saharan colony to achieve independence from European rule, Ward was determined to provide her audience with the knowledge needed to govern their newly founded country.

Her lectures, titled Five Ideas that Change the World, developed a world-historical narrative of the supposed human progress from nationalism to colonialism, industrialism, communism, and finally to internationalism, the highest point of political order.

Ghana’s peaceful democratic transition showed that African colonies were ready to govern themselves, weakening European arguments about the need for prolonged imperial guidance. The country soon became a model for new African statehood based on postcolonial sovereignty, inspiring other colonies on the continent to join the decolonisation process, which culminated in the ‘Year of Africa’ in 1960. The charismatic Nkrumah, who ruled Ghana from 1957 to 1966, became an international player in Cold War diplomacy by promoting pan-Africanist visions of post-imperial unity. He wanted to show the world that Africans were no longer imperial subjects but important and influential members of the global political community. While Nkrumah was a vociferous opponent of colonialism, Ward uncritically appreciated the civilisational and technical legacies of empire. Yet in her lectures, she supported Nkrumah’s international political aspirations by suggesting that economic development, international cooperation, and even world peace were interrelated problems that warranted a planetary solution.

Barbara Ward was a remarkable thinker, a visionary who imagined a ‘planetary’ political, economic and environmental justice based on both material and spiritual principles. She was an unusual figure in the Cold War political sphere, a charismatic public intellectual who advised world leaders and the United Nations at a time when women’s voices were often marginalised. She was among the first thinkers to argue that human prosperity, environmental sustainability and global justice were inseparable political questions. Her distinctive vision of planetary politics, grounded in ecological interdependence, moral responsibility and global cooperation, still offers insights into some of the most pressing challenges of the 21st century.

Ward’s diagnosis of Ghana’s predicament emerged from an intellectual trajectory that predated decolonisation itself. She was born in 1914 to a British Quaker-Catholic family that put a strong emphasis on education, encouraging her to attend a French lycée in Paris and later Somerville College, Oxford, where she was among the first women to graduate in politics, philosophy and economics in 1935. She continued to lecture at Oxford and Cambridge, as well as in Catholic circles, until 1939, when she launched her journalistic career as a contributor to The Economist on foreign affairs.
‘For 30 years, it has scarcely been possible to discuss development anywhere in the world without bringing in Barbara Ward’

During the war, Ward joined the Sword of the Spirit, then a British Catholic organisation that encouraged believers to support the democratic battle against totalitarianism. This experience, as well as her friendship with Arnold J Toynbee, Christopher Dawson and Jacques Maritain, persuaded her of the importance of religion – and especially Christianity – as the moral foundation of political and economic internationalism. Ward drew inspiration less from the doctrinal authority of the Catholic Church (which she frequently criticised as rigid and conservative) than from her own universalist interpretation of Christianity, which she regarded as a source of moral principles applicable to all humanity. Well beyond a personal creed, Ward’s Catholicism reflects a fundamental aspect of her political thought.

After the Second World War, Ward was interested in the global challenges of economic growth and reconstruction. She travelled extensively in the United States, India, Europe and Africa, where in 1946 she prepared a study of demography and migration in British Togoland. In 1950, she married the Australian civil servant Robert Jackson, and three years later the couple relocated to the Gold Coast, where Jackson was appointed chairman of the preparatory commission of the Volta Dam, one of the continent’s major economic-development projects.

Ward’s bestselling books and prestigious public lectures made her a well-known figure, and she developed a public profile as a political commentator and advisor to world leaders, including Nkrumah, Adlai Stevenson, John F Kennedy, Robert McNamara and Lyndon B Johnson. By the late 1950s, she divided her time between Harvard, where she held a visiting professorship, and Ghana, where she continued to promote the Volta Dam project, sharing Nkrumah’s hope that it might foster Ghana’s economic independence. Later, she was appointed to a prestigious professorship in development economics at Columbia University in New York, and in the 1970s she was made a Dame Commander of the Order of the British Empire and a life peer. Upon her death in 1981, The Washington Post acknowledged her influence by stating that: ‘For 30 years, it has scarcely been possible to discuss development anywhere in the world without bringing in Barbara Ward.’

Poverty was such a significant issue for Ward to tackle because it created global political unrest and undermined local societies’ potential to prosper. How could it be overcome? She was persuaded that only a revolution could help humanity undermine global inequality. The postwar era was, for her, a particularly promising time for radical change: ‘I suppose we are all aware of the fact that we live in the most catastrophically revolutionary age that men have ever faced.’ In the early 1960s, she identified ‘ten or twenty’ revolutions still underway. She singled out two important calls for equality: postcolonial self-determination, which led to ‘the new peoples’ claim to national equality with the older states’, and the revolution of economic development, which aimed to reduce global inequality. Following her friend Walt Rostow’s theory of modernisation, she explained that some countries (typically the European imperial powers) were ‘sensationally richer’ but others had ‘not yet’ realised a revolutionary transformation despite their ‘desire to do so’. The challenge of her era was to figure out how to make this revolution come true.

One successful ‘revolution’ was the Marshall Plan for the development of Europe after the Second World War, which Ward praised as an example of international economic planning. She suggested that Europe and the US should apply a similar model and provide financial aid to promote local economic development in India. Historically, Europe and the US prospered from the continuous plunder of colonial capital and resources. Imperialism caused ‘not only a considerable degree of political immaturity and instability’ but ‘also a type of economic structure or layout which is unlikely to produce further growth of itself’. For Ward, these structural inequalities in the world economy prevented postcolonial countries from overcoming poverty on their own.
Her proposals for the development of postcolonial societies expressed a paternalistic, hierarchical worldview

Ward outlined various measures to end economic inequality on a planetary scale: training local experts, transferring food surpluses to poorer countries, providing capital assistance in the form of a 1 per cent tax on national income, and advancing trade policies favourable to non-Western economies. Wealthy states, for Ward, should voluntarily embrace a more ambitious form of global fiscal redistribution because narrowing the world’s economic gap would benefit humanity as a whole. She maintained that encouraging economic growth in the ‘underdeveloped’ postcolonial world was in the West’s material interest. Yet, more importantly, it was its moral duty. Her proposals, pushing Cold War modernisation projects beyond strategic investment and reconstruction, struggled to generate political support at the time, but opened up discussions about the appropriate means to promote equality in the global economic order.

Ward accused Western societies of the ‘under-development’ of colonial societies but still considered the West superior to the rest of the world. She assumed that postcolonial countries wanted to follow Western industrialisation models (or in her terms, ‘to modernise’) but could not do so alone without Western guidance. Her proposals for the development of postcolonial societies expressed a paternalistic and hierarchical worldview. Moreover, by promoting a new world order based on ‘social justice, humane concern and Christian compassion’, Ward suggested that equality did not depend on material conditions alone but also on a spiritual transformation. In her political vision, Catholic universalism provided the foundational moral values for the realisation of a just political and economic order on a planetary scale.

Ward was fascinated by the planetary dimension of politics, which became central to her vision of development. The launch of the Soviet satellite Sputnik in 1957 inaugurated the Space Age, while Yuri Gagarin’s orbit of Earth in 1961 (and Valentina Tereshkova’s two years later) altered humanity’s perception of its place in the cosmos. As space exploration transformed public views of the limits of human life, and Planet Earth appeared as just one among many possible habitats for humanity, Ward argued that this new sense of unity would revolutionise human history. Her 1965 lectures at Columbia University, titled ‘Spaceship Earth’, outlined an idea of a fragile and united planet, anticipating the famous imagery generated in 1968 by ‘Earthrise’, William Anders’s iconic photo of Planet Earth from space. She was one of the first to argue that the Space Age would inaugurate a new kind of distinctively ‘planetary’ politics:

When the astronauts spin through more than a dozen sunrises and sunsets in a single day and night; when the whole globe lies below them with California one minute and Japan the next; when, as they return from space, they feel spontaneously, with the first Soviet spaceman: ‘How beautiful it is, our Earth’; it is inconceivable that no modification of consciousness or imagination occurs, no sense that quarrels are meaningless before the majestic yet vulnerable reality of a single planet carrying a single human species through infinite space.

Ward borrowed the metaphor ‘Spaceship Earth’ from the US inventor and scientist Buckminster Fuller, who used it in 1963 to describe the planet’s fragility. He argued that Earth was a capsule with limited resources on a ‘totally precarious’ vast space voyage, whose success depends on the rational actions of every single individual. Ward similarly suggested that:

Our planet is not much more than the capsule within which we have to live as human beings if we are to survive the vast space voyage upon which we have been engaged for hundreds of millennia – but without noticing yet our condition … We depend upon a little envelope of soil and a rather large envelope of atmosphere for life itself.

Yet, for her, the planetary perspective was not merely a celebration of extraterrestrial exploration but also an opportunity to highlight the limits of Cold War politics centred on the so-called ‘national interest’. The relevant scale of politics was planetary, not national. The challenges of global economic inequality could no longer be adequately addressed through national emancipation or self-determination, which limited political and economic change to state boundaries:

the logic of events – of economic interdependence, of ‘rising expectations’, of the neighbourhood of vast super-powers, of atomic risks – all point beyond the small community. The nationalist, in this age of a world society, may well be as obsolete as the dynast on the verge of the age of democracy.
She concluded that ‘we have become a single human community’ but warned that ‘Our physical unity has gone far ahead of our moral unity’.
Ward thought that only the Christian West could provide the world with the moral foundations of a planetary community

Technological changes, such as interconnectedness, shrinking space and industrialisation, were not enough to generate a meaningful political change. Ward argued that a planetary community could be achieved only by transforming the physical unity of Planet Earth into political, economic and potentially moral harmony. Yet identifying the appropriate moral foundations for planetary politics was a formidable challenge. She called for the emergence of a common planetary morality to ‘turn the mob into a community’.

Ward recognised the value of humanity’s pluralism yet, as a devout Catholic, she found inspiration in Christianity. She criticised the ecclesiastical institutions, although she was one of the few women in 1964 invited to contribute her expertise to the Second Vatican Council, and admitted that, historically, faith had ‘divided the world so bitterly’. But she was persuaded that the notion of ‘Christian brotherhood’ could help rediscover ‘what unites rather than divides the communities of the world’. Quoting Pope Paul VI, she argued that the newly found unity of her era emerged from ‘one of the fundamental moral insights of the Western culture which has now swept over the whole globe’, namely that ‘mankind is not a group of warring tribes, but a single, equal and fraternal community’. Equality and justice thus relied on the ‘Western sense that men, as souls of infinite metaphysical value, stand equal before the throne of God’.

Thus, in the mid-1960s, Ward uncritically sought to persuade her audience that only the Christian West could provide the world with the moral foundations of a planetary community. The ‘West’ had a special responsibility, she argued, to provide moral guidance for a new world order based on justice, equality and solidarity. Thus, the Christian West was self-servingly represented as both fraternal and paternal, both equal and superior, and a cultivator of a universal creed that could motivate planetary action. Imagining a ‘planetary community’ that could foster humanity’s freedom and equality was, for Ward, an act of faith.

Alongside economic inequality and planetary politics, the third pillar of Ward’s thought regards humanity’s relations with the natural environment. In the 1970s, she used the term ‘sustainable development’ to argue that economic growth, though essential to human wellbeing, must not come at the cost of natural degradation. She outlined a vision for sustainable growth that reflected her optimism about ending poverty while avoiding a planetary economic and environmental crisis.

In the early 1970s, Ward offered an original and optimistic response to two contemporaneous concerns about growth. Thinkers in the Global South worried that there was not enough economic growth to generate wealth and prosperity in postcolonial countries. Without robust economic growth, these new states could not guarantee welfare services, healthcare and education to their citizens. Economic stagnation could threaten political stability and peace, always a significant concern during the Cold War. At the same time, Western thinkers warned that the relentless pursuit of economic growth in consumerist societies was destroying the natural environment. In 1972, the Club of Rome published its report, The Limits to Growth, endorsing plans of economic equilibrium rather than growth as a strategy for planetary ecological wellbeing.

Ward rejected the catastrophic pessimism of her fellow economists, who challenged existing growth models, but echoed their concerns about the planet as a fragile, vulnerable environment that needed to be preserved for future generations. Moreover, she was sympathetic to the claims of ‘developing countries to get their peoples out of a trap of poverty’ through economic growth based on agricultural and industrial innovation. Yet she did not think that these two aims – economic and environmental justice – were necessarily at odds. Optimistically, she suggested that economic wellbeing and planetary wellbeing could be reconciled if humanity acted collectively, morally and responsibly.
Ward underlined the importance of knowledge in politics

Ward’s vision achieved its clearest expression in 1972, at the UN Conference on the Human Environment, which was the international organisation’s first attempt to outline a common environmental strategy for the world. Ward was invited to take a leading role in preparation for the conference in Stockholm and wrote (with the scientist René Dubos) the report Only One Earth: The Care and Maintenance of a Small Planet, which was circulated to all participants before the event to present the organisers’ vision of economic development with respect for nature.

Drawing on her vast international network of experts, Ward approached 152 scientists, diplomats, industry leaders and stakeholders from 58 countries, and solicited their views about the prospects of economic development and its impact on the planet. She wanted to give space to the multiple, sometimes contradictory, opinions about the ecological impact of economic-growth strategies. She edited the collected ideas into a comprehensive document outlining possible approaches to ensure that economic growth wouldn’t come at the expense of the biosphere by limiting (though not banning) pollution, consumption and extraction.

The book concluded with a vision of a ‘planetary order’, premised on a ‘shared biosphere’ in which humanity had to use technology to survive. Planetary politics was not just about a world scale, but also about paying attention to the long-term impact of political choices on the physical conditions of Planet Earth. Thus, Ward underlined the importance of knowledge in politics: while scientists and experts should not replace politicians in national or international governance, they should provide the necessary data for informed decision-making:

The first step towards devising a strategy for Planet Earth is for the nations to accept a collective responsibility for discovering more – much more – about the natural system and how it is affected by man’s activities and vice-versa.

Financial investment, international cooperation, and scientific expertise could help ‘creep up on the infinitely sensitive issues of divisive economic and political sovereignty’ because ‘No nations, on their own, can offset the risk of deepening disorder.’

International governance could, Ward argued, provide the best means for overcoming environmental degradation and economic inequality. Yet, at the conference, she discovered that not all members of the UN wanted to limit national sovereignty. Her plans to expand international cooperation to the non-violent settlement of disputes, progressive farming, urban planning, pollution control and global economic redistribution remained on paper. While largely unrealised, the declaration that the conference’s delegates produced remained an important signpost on the road towards global environmental governance.
She later downplayed her earlier emphasis on Christianity as the moral foundation for a planetary community

Ward advocated for institutional innovation on a planetary scale and considered the UN as a proto-world government. Yet she was acutely aware of the limits of international institutions and, by the late 1970s, lamented the UN’s inability to translate environmental commitments into effective action. The challenge was not just to create adequate institutions, but also to give them the power to act. In this sense, Ward suspected that the problem was not the institution’s design but the ‘loyalties’ of its members, which were based on ideology and morality: ‘The planet is not yet a centre of rational loyalty for all of mankind.’ Instead of institutional change, she sought to transform the world’s civil society by raising public consciousness of questions of political and economic justice. A new planetary order should be based not on top-down institutions but on a bottom-up planetary community that ‘our environmental interdependence’ could generate.

To fully appreciate Ward’s contribution, it is important to acknowledge the limits of her vision. Her viewpoint was inherently Western-centric and elitist, and her earlier writings frequently explained imperial expansion as an expression of Europe’s civilising mission. She advanced a civilisational hierarchy that viewed Christianity as the ethical basis of human unity, undermining alternative creeds. Areas of the world that she dubbed ‘undeveloped’ were assigned only a passive role in her planetary community. When the ‘Global South’ sought to shape its own political and economic future through initiatives such as the New International Economic Order, she insisted that the West still had a moral responsibility to lead the transition to global justice and equality.

It is worth noticing, however, that in her later writings about environmental justice, Ward downplayed her earlier emphasis on Christianity as the moral foundation for a planetary community, suggesting instead that public awareness of the planet’s physical unity could also generate political union. Economic development of postcolonial countries should, she argued in the 1970s, take local preferences into account rather than follow a Western model. The emergence of ecological concerns marked a significant shift in Ward’s political thought, transforming her understanding of the relationship between economic justice, political unity and postcolonial world order.

Ward remains relevant today as a far-sighted thinker who anticipated the intertwined challenges of inequality, environmental degradation and global governance that continue to dominate political debates. In her later writings about the environment, she advanced a more inclusive idea of planetary community based on ‘physical interconnectedness’ and postcolonial self-determination, abandoning some of her earlier ideas about Christian morality and European superiority. By outlining a vision to end global inequality, protect nature from harm and generate economic growth, Ward sought to save humanity from its own demise. Her ambitions were matched only by her optimism that her vision of a planetary community of welfare, growth and harmony with nature would, one day, be realised.
